processing: Withered first, then kill-green, rolling, sealed yellowing (men huang) and drying. The withering before the kill and the yellowing after rolling take off grassy, astringent edges.
harvest_season: One bud with two to three leaves; a large, mature pluck compared with bud-style yellow teas. Season is less well documented; as with most Chinese teas, spring is usually favoured.
appearance_dry: Plump, tight, heavy strands of fairly even maturity, large for a yellow tea.
appearance_wet: Broad, large, soft leaves in a yellow-green.
taste_profile: Mellow, smooth and rounded with a mild sweetness and returning aftertaste; the aroma is described as floral and fruity, with some smokiness.

brewing.notes: Use 80–85°C water; three or four steeps is the usual stamina. Boiling water brings out roughness in the large leaf.

vintage_note: Usually sold as current-year tea, as is common for yellow teas, and meant for drinking within a year or so. Harvest details are not always stated, so ask for the year; it is not a tea with an ageing market.
description:
Guangdong Da Ye Qing, big-leaf green, is the southern outlier among yellow teas. Unlike bud teas such as Junshan Yinzhen, it belongs to the large-leaf 'huang da cha' group and uses Yunnan large-leaf plants grown in Guangdong. Shaoguan, Zhaoqing and Zhanjiang are the areas named most often, and Meizhou and Qingyuan also appear.

The method has an unusual step: the leaf is withered before the kill-green, which most yellow teas skip. Then comes rolling and the sealed yellowing that defines the class. Together, those stages knock back the grassy, astringent bite you would expect from big leaf.

Expect a soft, mellow cup in yellow to orange-yellow, with some sweetness and a returning aftertaste. Keep the water around 80–85°C and do not expect a long gongfu session: three or four steeps is normal.

This is an everyday tea more than a collectible. Look for even, plump strands and a clean smell. Descriptions of the leaf shape vary, with some calling it flat and most calling it tight and strip-like, so judge by the sample rather than the words on a page.
history: Little is documented about when this tea first appeared or who developed it. It is described as a traditional Guangdong yellow tea and as a leading example of the large-leaf yellow group, and one tea reference reports it as a provincial intangible heritage item, a claim worth treating as unconfirmed.
